lesson.title: From Data to Variance: The Step by Step Formula
lesson.summary: Calculating variance follows a fixed sequence of steps: find the mean, subtract it from each value, square each deviation, and average the squares, with the averaging divisor depending on whether the data represent a full population or a sample.
lesson.body:
Now that you know what variance means and why it is built from squared deviations, the calculation itself is a short, repeatable sequence of steps. Step one, find the mean of the data set. Step two, subtract the mean from every individual value to get each value's deviation. Step three, square every deviation so that all values become positive. Step four, add up the squared deviations. Step five, divide that sum by an appropriate count to get the average squared deviation, which is the variance.

That last step is where population and sample data are treated differently, and the distinction matters. If your data set is an entire population, meaning every member of the group you care about, you divide the sum of squared deviations by N, the population size, and the result is called the population variance, written with the symbol sigma squared. If your data set is a sample meant to represent a larger population, you divide by n minus 1 instead of n, and the result is called the sample variance, written s squared. Dividing by n minus 1 rather than n is a deliberate correction, sometimes called Bessel's correction, that makes the sample variance a better, unbiased estimate of the true population variance, because a sample's own mean is always at least as close to its own data as the true population mean would be.

Suppose a teacher records quiz scores for an entire class of 5 students, meaning this is a full population: 7, 9, 10, 12, and 12. The mean is 7 plus 9 plus 10 plus 12 plus 12, divided by 5, which is 50 divided by 5, or 10. The deviations from the mean are -3, -1, 0, 2, and 2. Squaring each gives 9, 1, 0, 4, and 4, which sum to 18. Because this is the entire population, divide by N, which is 5, giving a population variance of 18 divided by 5, or 3.6, and a population standard deviation of the square root of 3.6, approximately 1.90.

Now suppose that same set of five scores was only a sample drawn from a much larger group of students, not the whole population. The sum of squared deviations is still 18, but now you divide by n minus 1, which is 4, giving a sample variance of 18 divided by 4, or 4.5, and a sample standard deviation of the square root of 4.5, approximately 2.12. Notice that the sample calculation, dividing by a smaller number, always produces a variance at least as large as the population calculation on the same numbers; this is exactly the correction working as intended.

In an AP Statistics course, you will almost always be told, or need to infer from context, whether your data represent a population or a sample, since that single choice changes the divisor and therefore the final answer. Most real studies work with samples, so s squared and s are the versions you will use most often in practice, while sigma squared and sigma describe the population values that a good sample is trying to estimate.
